sentences.text: What if your AI never had to search?
Cache-augmented generation, CAG, loads a whole knowledge base into the model once, keeps the model's memory of it, and answers every question without a retrieval step.
I tested it against RAG on my own machine, with real numbers.
It works.
But what decided whether it works wasn't the trick.
It was the size of the model.
RAG looks up a few relevant passages for every question.
CAG skips the lookup.
You put the entire knowledge base into the prompt once, and the model computes its internal memory of that text, the KV cache.
Every later question reuses that memory, so only the question itself has to be read.
The catch: everything must fit in the model's context window, everyone gets the same text, and the first request is slow.
It suits a small, stable knowledge base that people ask about a lot.
Everything here is local.
Ollama, a Qwen eight-billion model and a Qwen thirty-two-billion model, on one MacBook, no cloud API.
The knowledge base is a slice of Ollama's own documentation: a hundred and eighteen sections, about twenty-six thousand tokens.
I built this with an AI coding assistant, and it wrote the ninety test questions.
Fifty-one of them ask about things the documentation never says, because the right answer to those is: not in the knowledge base.
Forty questions for development, fifty held back.
No human reviewed them.
I'll come back to that.
First question: does the cache actually work?
Here is the eight-billion model on the documentation.
The first call has to read all twenty-six thousand tokens, which took me between two and three minutes.
After that, reading the prompt takes a fraction of a second, because more than ninety-nine percent of it comes from the cache.
With the thirty-two-billion model that first call takes eight and a half minutes.
That cold start is the real price of CAG.
My first surprise.
The cache lives inside Ollama, and one Ollama server has exactly one slot for it.
When I loaded a second model for chat, it pushed the cache out, and the next question paid the full cold start again, sixty-five seconds in that test.
The fix was a dedicated Ollama server for the cached model.
Now the result, on the fifty held-out questions.
The eight-billion model with CAG got twenty-eight percent right.
It answered thirty-six of the forty questions the documentation can't answer, inventing details instead of saying it didn't know.
RAG with the same small model got eighty-four.
The thirty-two-billion model with CAG got ninety-eight percent, refused all forty unanswerable questions, and answered in three seconds, where RAG on the same model takes nineteen.
Same trick, same data.
The difference was the size of the model.
I tried to make answers traceable by telling the model to quote its sources.
Citations went from five percent to sixty-five percent.
But the small model started inventing evidence.
Asked about mutual TLS, which the documentation never mentions, it wrote a sentence that isn't in the documentation and pinned it on a real section.
So I stopped asking the model.
After it answers, I find the supporting section by matching the answer against the documents.
That found the right section ninety-three to a hundred percent of the time.
The next surprise was about my own measurements.
On the first forty questions, a semantic similarity check looked like the best way to catch invented answers.
Then I wrote fifty new questions, and it flipped: the simple word-overlap check won.
Forty questions had been too few to choose a method.
The small model's refusal rate told the same story: twenty-seven percent on the first set, ten percent on the new one.
Always keep questions you haven't tuned on.
A production service has to survive failures.
So I killed Ollama in the middle of a request.
The caller got an error in under a tenth of a second.

The health check stayed up, readiness switched to not ready, and when I restarted Ollama the service re-read the whole knowledge base by itself and recovered, in two and a half minutes for the small model.
For the big one, just re-reading takes eight and a half minutes, so you would want a second copy running.
Then I attacked it.
I hid instructions inside the documents.
Neither model obeyed a command like ignore your rules, but the bigger one followed a hidden instruction once and added a tracking link, and both repeated a false fact I planted as if it were true.
No prompt fixes that: you have to control what goes into the knowledge base.
A test asking for planted emails, card numbers and keys got all five back, until I added redaction.
And under load the service handles about five requests a minute however many people ask, so now it turns the extras away in ten milliseconds.
Last, I wanted to catch regressions.
A gate re-runs the questions and fails if accuracy or abstention drops below thresholds taken from the held-out results.
It also locks the knowledge base and the prompt: change one fact in the documentation and the check fails until you re-run the full evaluation.
It runs in seconds, and a secret scanner checks every push.
Five things.
One: CAG fits a small, stable knowledge base that gets asked about a lot.
Two: the cache is the product, so budget for the cold start.
Three: model size mattered more than any trick I tried.
Four: measure what happens on questions the knowledge base can't answer.
Five: keep questions you didn't tune on.
Everything here is local and open, with the caveats stated: one machine, ninety questions written by an AI, no human review.
